Adoniram Judson
uh-DON-ih-ram JUD-suhn
proper noun (person)
First American foreign missionary (1788-1850), pioneer to Burma and translator of the Burmese Bible.

📖 Biblical Definition

Adoniram Judson was the first American foreign missionary, the pioneer of the gospel in Burma, and one of the great sufferers in the history of missions. Sent out in 1812, he and his wife Ann labored for years before seeing a single convert, learning the Burmese language and translating the Scriptures. Judson gave his life to rendering the whole Bible into Burmese, a labor of decades that remains the standard translation among Burmese Christians to this day. His path was marked by terrible affliction: imprisonment for nearly two years in the death-prison of Ava during war, chained and tormented; the deaths of two wives and several children; recurring sickness and grief that drove him at times to the edge of despair. Yet he pressed on, and from his perseverance came a thriving Burmese church, especially among the Karen people, that endures and grows to this day. Judson stands in the dictionary as the suffering pioneer of Burma, who counted no anguish too great to give the Scriptures and the gospel to a people without Christ, and whose labors, watered with tears and blood, brought forth a harvest that has outlasted his every sorrow.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

First American foreign missionary (1788-1850), pioneer to Burma and translator of the Burmese Bible; who through imprisonment, the loss of wives and children, and years without converts laid the foundation of an enduring Burmese church.

ADONIRAM JUDSON, proper noun. First American foreign missionary (1788-1850).

Pioneer of the gospel in Burma from 1812.

Translator of the whole Bible into Burmese, still the standard version.

Imprisoned nearly two years in the death-prison of Ava; lost two wives and children.

Labored years before the first convert; left a thriving Burmese and Karen church.

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 126:6 — "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him."

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Acts 14:22 — "...we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God."

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Judson's life honors the recovery of perseverance in missions and the necessity of the gospel for the unreached, against a religion that shrinks from suffering and a pluralism that denies the nations need Christ.

expand to see more

Pluralism correction. A modern pluralism insists that the nations have their own religions and need not the gospel of Christ, making missions an arrogant intrusion. Judson's life answers from Scripture: how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard (Rom 10:14)? The dictionary holds the necessity and exclusivity of Christ — there is salvation in no other name — and commends the missionary's conviction that the unreached must hear, whatever the cost to the messenger.

This entry faces little further postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is perseverance through suffering and delay. Judson labored years without a convert, buried wives and children, and endured the horrors of Ava's prison, yet did not quit. The dictionary commends his steadfastness: those who sow the precious seed in tears shall doubtless come again rejoicing, bringing their sheaves (Psa 126:6). The Burmese church today is the harvest of his refusal to give up.
